Two-step anaerobic digestion of rice straw with nanobubble water 
Enzhen Wang a, Hui Sun b, Penghui Chen a, Yonghui Zheng a, Jianbin Guo a,*, Renjie Dong a 
a College of Engineering (Key Laboratory for Clean Renewable Energy Utilization Technology, Ministry of Agriculture), China Agricultural University, Beijing 100083, PR 
China 
b College of Mechanical & Electrical Engineering, Henan Agricultural University, Zhengzhou 450002, PR China   
H I G H L I G H T S  
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T  
• Nanobubble water (NW) as soaking 
agent and AD accelerant was studied. 
• Methane yield of straw with NW 
increased by 11.0%–21.4% compared 
with untreated. 
• NW soaking enhanced volatile fatty 
acids production by 78.9%–214.4%. 
• NW as AD accelerant increased relative 
abundance of Methanosaeta.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Methane production 
Nanobubble water 
Soaking pretreatment 
Accelerant 
Microbial community 
A B S T R A C T   
Lignocellulose usually requires pretreatment to improve biogas production. To enhance lignocellulose biode­
gradability and improve anaerobic digestion (AD) efficiency, different types (N2, CO2, and O2) of nanobubble 
water (NW) were applied in this study as soaking agent and AD accelerant to increase the biogas yield of rice 
straw. The results showed that the cumulative methane yields of treating with NW in two-step AD increased by 
11.0%–21.4% compared with untreated straw. The maximum cumulative methane yield was 313.9±1.7 mL/gVS 
in straw treated with CO2-NW as soaking agent and AD accelerant (PCO2-MCO2). The application of CO2-NW and 
O2-NW as AD accelerants increased bacterial diversity and relative abundance of Methanosaeta. This study 
suggested that using NW could enhance soaking pretreatment and methane production of rice straw in two-step 
AD; however, combined treatment with inoculum and NW or microbubble water in the pretreatment needs to 
compare in future.   
1. Introduction 
A total of 970 million tonnes of crop straw is produced annually in 
China, which causes serious environmental pollution and resource waste 
if not disposed of properly (Sun et al., 2021). Anaerobic digestion (AD) 
of straw is an agricultural waste treatment technology that has been 
widely applied, as it can simultaneously recover biogas as energy and 
digestate as organic fertilizer, alleviate the crisis of fossil energy

shortages, and reduce carbon emissions (Cai et al., 2021). 
To enhance the biogas production from lignocellulosic materials, 
many studies have been conducted focusing on pretreatments to over­
come their complex and refractory lignocellulosic structure (Yu et al., 
2019). At present, straw pretreatment methods are mainly physical 
(milling, extrusion, ultrasonic pretreatment, steam explosion pretreat­
ment, and thermal hydrolysis), chemical (alkaline pretreatment and acid 
pretreatment), and biological (fungi) (Shrestha et al., 2017). Although 
the degradability of lignocellulose is improved after pretreatment, each 
type of pretreatment has its advantages and disadvantages. For example, 
physical pretreatment is easy to implement, but has high energy de­
mand; chemical pretreatment has high efficiency, but is associated with 
pollutant or inhibitory compounds; and biological pretreatment is cost- 
effective, but has long pretreatment cycle (Cai et al., 2021; Guan et al., 
2022; Ma et al., 2022). These limitations raise the need to explore more 
efficient pretreatment methods with lower energy consumption and 
fewer chemical additives. 
Nanobubble water (NW) has defined as bubbles <1000 nm in 
diameter (ISO/TC281) and generated in water by mechanical stirring, 
hydraulic cavitation, ultrasonic cavitation, dissolved gas release, and 
membrane filtration etc. (Wang et al., 2021b). In recent years, NW has 
been widely applied in wastewater treatment (Xiao et al., 2021), 
membrane cleaning (Farid et al., 2022), aquaculture (Liu et al., 2013), 
irrigation (Zhou et al., 2022), and waste disposal (Fan et al., 2021). The 
interest in nanobubble is due to their unique characteristics, such as 
their long residence time in solution, high zeta potential compared with 
deionized water (DW), possible ability to generate hydroxyl radicals, 
and high gas-liquid mass transfer efficiency compared with micro­
bubbles which size range is 1–100 μm (Chuenchart et al., 2021; Wang 
et al., 2021b). Experimental evidence has demonstrated the long-term 
existence of nanobubbles; however, the mechanism behind their long- 
term existence remains controversial. 
Although the benefits of NW as AD accelerant have been confirmed, 
the mechanism by which NW promotes AD is unclear. Some researchers 
have reported that adding NW to AD reactors with waste activated 
sludge, pig manure, food waste, and corn straw as feedstock could in­
crease the biogas yields by 3% – 40% compared with the addition of DW 
(Chuenchart et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020b; Yang et al., 2019). These 
positive effects of NW addition may be attributed to improved AD per­
formance and efficiency, which promotes substrate biodegradation (Fan 
et al., 2020a), prevents acid accumulation (Fan et al., 2020b), and al­
leviates ammonia inhibition (Fan et al., 2021). In addition, some pre­
dictions have been put forward based on research results. Negatively 
charged nanobubbles enhance the mobility of water molecules which is 
related to the mass transfer rate of nutrients from liquid to cells (Wang 
et al., 2019). This also means that mass transfer between microorgan­
isms and the environment is accelerated when NW is used in an AD 
system. Thus, the addition of NW to an AD reactor could enhance their 
enzymatic activity and increase the relative abundance of major func­
tional bacteria and archaea (Wang et al., 2020a). 
There are only a few studies on the addition of NW in the AD process, 
while there was no comprehensive evaluation of applying NW to two- 
step AD process with soaking pretreatment and methane production. 
Therefore, the main purpose of this study was to clarify the various 
contributions of NW in two-step AD with soaking pretreatment and 
methane production. Initially, this study evaluated the effect of soaking 
pretreatment with different types of NW (N2-NW, CO2-NW, and O2-NW) 
on the hydrolysis efficiency of air-dried rice straw. Following the pre­
treatment, the effect of NW as an AD accelerant on biogas production 
was also examined. In brief, the purpose of this study was to explore the 
effects of different types of NW on the hydrolysis performance and 
biogas production of air-dried rice straw with the aim of providing an 
efficient method for improving the biogas production of air-dried rice 
straw without the addition of hazardous chemical substances. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Rice straw and inoculum 
Rice straw was harvested from a farm in the Hubei Province, China 
(31◦43′N, 112◦07′E). The straw was sheared and stored in a laboratory 
freezer at 4 ◦C. Before being fed into the anaerobic reactor, the straw was 
cut to 1–2 cm in length using a straw chopper. The inoculum was ob­
tained from mesophilic anaerobic digester operated stably in a munic­
ipal wastewater treatment plant in Beijing. The sludge was placed in a 
reactor at 37 ◦C for one week until no biogas was produced and then 
used for the batch AD experiments. The characteristics of rice straw and 
inoculum are shown in Table 1. 
2.2. Preparation of nanobubble water 
Briefly, NW was generated using N2, CO2, or O2 gas (purity >99.9%, 
Beijing Haipu Gas Co., Ltd., China) and DW by a micro-nanobubble 
rapid generation device (TL-MBG10-A, Beijing Zhongnongtianlu Co., 
Ltd., China). NW was generated in the gas-liquid mixing tank of the 
generator through the hydraulic cavitation formed by the high-speed 
rotating shearing of the circulated water pump, and then released into 
the water tank through a nozzle ready for testing and use. The NW was 
placed for 3–5 min after preparation to make most of macro/micro­
bubble to escape from the water, during which freshly prepared water 
gradually changed from milky white to transparent. 
Some studies have shown that the concentration of bubbles in NW 
was significantly affected by the operating time of the device (Cerron- 
Calle et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019). Therefore, the effect of operating 
time (5, 10, 15, and 20 min) on nanobubbles concentration and size 
distribution was explored under the settings of 1 L/min of gas intake and 
20 L of water volume in the tank. For the O2-NW and N2-NW, the 
nanobubble concentration increased to 3.8×108 ± 3.7×107 and 
1.43×108 ± 1.5×107 particles/mL within 15 min, respectively. The 
concentration became unstable (temperature of water rises as the device 
runs for a long time) over the following 5 min. However, for the CO2- 
NW, the highest concentration of nanobubble was observed at 10 min 
(1.1×108 ± 1.0×107 particles/mL). After 10 min, the concentration 
decreased with operation time (see supplementary material). Therefore, 
the operation times for generating O2-NW and N2-NW were 15 min, and 
that for generating the CO2-NW was 10 min. 
2.3. Soaking pretreatment of rice straw 
To explore the effect of soaking pretreatment with different types of 
NW on the hydrolysis of rice straw, experiments were conducted with 
four types of soaking water: DW, N2-NW, CO2-NW, and O2-NW, and the 
treatment groups were labeled as PDW, PN2, PCO2, and PO2, respectively. 
The solid-liquid ratio of rice straw to water was 1:10 based on the total 
solids (TS) in a 250-mL glass bottle. To avoid organic matter loss under 
aerobic conditions during the soaking process, the headspace of the 
bottle was flushed with N2 for 1 min and immediately sealed with a 
nitrile stopper after the addition of water and rice straw. All glass bottles 
were placed in a constant temperature incubator (RZH-380A, Nanbei

Co., Ltd., China) at 37±1 ◦C for 5 d. All bottles were shaken by hand for 
30 s every day. Fifteen bottles were included in each treatment: three 
bottles were used for material characteristic analysis after 5 d of soaking, 
and twelve bottles were used for subsequent batch AD experiments. 
2.4. Set-up of batch AD experiment for rice straw 
The inoculum was loaded directly into the soaking bottles with a 
substrate-to-inoculum based on the volatile solids (VS) ratio of was 1:1.5 
after 5 days of soaking. Subsequently, different types of NW were sup­
plemented as AD accelerants to maintain same TS in the bottles, and the 
treatment groups were labeled as MN2, MCO2, and MO2, respectively. DW 
was also added to the AD reactor, maintaining the same TS (labeled as 
MDW). Unsoaked rice straw supplemented with DW was used as un­
treated group. The biogas production of the inoculum alone was also 
determined (labeled as blank group) (see supplementary material). After 
loading, the headspace of the bottle was flushed with N2 for 1 min and 
then immediately sealed. All bottles were placed at 37±1 ◦C in a con­
stant temperature water bath (HH-60, Changzhou Guohua Co., Ltd., 
China) and shaken by hand for 30 s every day. Three replicates were set 
for each treatment, and the actual biogas production of the rice straw 
was calculated by subtracting the biogas production of the blank group 
from that of the treatment groups. 
2.5. Analytical methods 
TS and VS were measured according to the standard methods of the 
American Public Health Association (APHA, 2005). The pH was 
measured using a pH meter (FE28, Mettler-Toledo, Switzerland). Cel­
lulose, hemicellulose, and acid detergent lignin contents were deter­
mined using a fiber analyzer (2000, Ankom Technology Corp., USA) 
according to Vansoest (1963). Crystallinity was measured using an X-ray 
diffractometer (D8, Bruker, Germany), and the relevant parameters 
were set according to Gao et al. (2017). The crystallinity index (CrI) 
calculation formula is shown in Eq. (1). 
CrI(%) = [(I002 −Iam)/I002] × 100%
(1)  
where I002 is the maximum intensity at 2θ angles of 22◦–23◦, and Iam is 
the intensity of the amorphous structure in the 2θ range of 16◦–18◦. 
The size and concentration of nanobubbles were determined using a 
Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis (NTA) device (NanoSight NS500, Mal­
vern, UK), which generally provides the particle size distribution of the 
sample in liquid based on light scattering and Brownian motion analyses 
(Kestens et al., 2017). A high sensitivity CMOS camera recorded videos 
of the Brownian motion of the nanobubble; subsequently, their Brow­
nian motion was analyzed by the NTA software to obtain particle size 
distribution and concentration. The device was flushed to ensure that 
there were no obvious particles by the camera before detection. The 
camera level and focus were adjusted to obtain the maximum image 
after loading each sample. Capture number was set to three times in each 
case. 
The volume of daily biogas production was measured using a glass 
syringe; the syringe was inserted to the bottles, and the volume was 
recorded once it stabilized. The volume was subsequently normalized to 
the standard temperature and pressure conditions. Biogas composition 
was measured via gas chromatography (GC8A, Shimadzu, Japan). Vol­
atile fatty acids (VFAs) concentrations were analyzed by gas chroma­
tography (GC-2010 Plus, Shimadzu, Japan). The modified Gompertz 
model was used to analyze the kinetic characteristics of different groups 
of methane production. The model is shown as in Eq. (2). 
P(t) = P0 × exp

the delay phase (d); and t is the time of AD (d). 
2.6. Microbial community analysis 
To further explore the effect of adding NW as AD accelerant on mi­
crobial community, samples from the PDW-MDW, PDW-MN2, PDW-MCO2, 
PDW-MO2, and PCO2-MCO2 treatments were collected and centrifuged for 
microbial community analyses. DNA was extracted using an E.Z.N.A.® 
Soil DNA Kit (Omega Bio-tek, Norcross, GA, USA) according to the 
manufacturer’s protocols, while 1% agarose gel electrophoresis was 
used to check DNA quality. The 16S rRNA gene primers used were 338F 
and 806R for bacteria and 524F10extF and Arch958RmodR for archaea. 
The sequence was detected on Illumina MiSeq platform device (Illu­
mina, San Diego, USA) at the Majorbio bio-Pharm Technology Co., Ltd. 
(Shanghai, China). Specific operational procedures and microbial com­
munity analysis methods were referred to previous studies (Sun et al., 
2019). The microbial community diversity and distribution were 
analyzed using the Majorbio Cloud Platform (https://www.majorbio. 
com). The raw sequencing data were submitted to the Sequence Read 
Archive (SRA) of National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) 
under project number PRJNA935990. 
2.7. Data analysis 
In this study, graph processing and model analysis were performed 
using Origin 2021 (OriginLab, USA). Significant differences were 
determined by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) using SPSS 25 
software. Statistical significance was assumed at p < 0.05. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Effect of soaking pretreatment on rice straw with nanobubble water 
3.1.1. Volatile fatty acids production after soaking pretreatment 
As shown in Fig. 1, the total VFAs concentrations in the treatments of 
PDW, PN2, PCO2, and PO2 were 1873.3±242.5, 3351.4±117.2, 5889.6 
±928.0, and 3782.6±270.8 mg-HAc/L, respectively, after 5-days of 
soaking pretreatment. The results indicated that soaking pretreatment in 
NW significantly increased the total VFAs concentration of soaking 
liquid (p < 0.05). Particularly, acetic acid concentration significantly 
increased in the soaking of the NW treatment (p < 0.05). And the highest

acetic acid production (4221.8±870.6 mg-HAc/L) was observed in the 
treatment of PCO2, which was 5.4-fold that in the PDW treatment (655.5 
±183.0 mg-HAc/L). Likewise, acetic acid concentration reached 2079.4 
±74.5 and 2393.8±74.8 mg-HAc/L in the treatments of PN2 and PO2, 
which was 2.2-fold and 2.6-fold that of the PDW treatment, respectively. 
To date, most studies have focused on improving hydrolysis effi­
ciency through NW addition in the AD process. Yang et al. (2019) found 
that when N2-NW was added to AD process of waste activated sludge, 
the VFAs concentration increased by 31.4% after the initial three days 
compared with the addition of DW. Wang et al. (2020a) observed that 
the addition of Air-NW and CO2-NW to a high cellulose loading AD 
reactor increased VFAs concentrations by 30.3% and 11.4%, respec­
tively, compared with the addition of DW. Some researchers have shown 
that the addition of NW changed the microscale water environment of 
the AD system and accelerated water mobility, which was an important 
factor affecting the hydrolysis process (Wang et al., 2019). With an in­
crease in water mobility, the flow rate of substances and energy between 
microorganisms and the outside environment was enhanced and the 
release of enzymes was elevated, which was beneficial to the hydrolysis 
of substances (Chuenchart et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020b). In this 
study, no exogenous hydrolytic bacteria were inoculated in the soaking 
pretreatment, and only epiphytic bacteria were present in the straw. 
Although no hydrolytic microorganisms were added to enhance hy­
drolysis in the AD process, the soaking pretreatment functioned as a pre- 
hydrolysis process. In this case, rice straw soaked in NW showed 78.9%– 
214.4% increases in VFAs production compared with that soaked in DW. 
Thus, coupling with NW and exogenous hydrolytic bacterial inoculum is 
speculated to further increase the VFAs production. 
In addition, CO2-NW exhibited unique characteristics. Compared 
with N2-NW and O2-NW, a large amount of CO2 was dissolved into water 
to form carbonic acid in CO2-NW. The low pH of CO2-NW (i.e., 4.2) 
created an acidic environment which might explain why the highest 
VFAs production was observed in the PCO2 treatment (Wang et al., 
2019). In addition, the increased acetic acid content in the PCO2 treat­
ment would be good for the subsequent AD process, because acetic acid 
could be directly utilized by methanogens as the main energy source (Li 
et al., 2022). 
3.1.2. Lignocellulose content and crystallinity index of rice straw after 
soaking 
The contents of cellulose, hemicellulose, and acid detergent lignin in 
rice straw after soaking pretreatment are shown in Table 2. The cellulose 
content in treatments of the untreated, PDW, PN2, PCO2 and PO2 were 
26.2% ± 0.6%, 27.2% ± 0.6%, 27.2% ± 0.5%, 28.4% ± 0.2%, and 
28.5% ± 0.4%, respectively. Compared with that in the untreated 
group, the cellulose content increased significantly after soaking (p <
0.05), showing an increase of 3.8%, 3.8%, 8.4%, and 8.8%, respectively. 
Crystallinity was also an important factor in the hydrolysis of rice straw. 
The CrI of rice straw was 43.9%, 43.7%, 48.2%, and 44.7% in the 
treatments soaked in DW, N2-NW, CO2-NW, and O2-NW, respectively, all 
of which was higher than that in the untreated group (40.2%). 
These results might be due to the stronger resistance in the crystal­
line region of cellulose than that in the amorphous region, and the 
degradation of part of the amorphous cellulose and hemicellulose during 
soaking (Ma et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2017). Therefore, 
part of the amorphous material was dissolved, thus destructing the 
complex and refractory lignocellulose structure to some extent and 
increasing the accessibility of the enzymes to cellulose, which was 
beneficial for increasing biogas production. 
3.2. Effect of methane production on rice straw with nanobubbles water 
The effect of sole soaking pretreatment with different types of NW on 
the methane production of rice straw is illustrated in Fig. 2. Sole soaking 
pretreatment in either DW or NW (PDW-MDW, PN2-MDW, PCO2-MDW, or 
PO2-MDW) significantly increased the cumulative methane yields by 
11.8%–14.2% (288.9–295.1 mL/gVS, p < 0.05) compared with that in 
the untreated group (258.5±1.8 mL/gVS). However, the improvement 
was comparable between the NW and the DW soaking treatment (p >
0.05) (Fig. 2). It was obvious that the higher peak of daily methane yield 
after soaking pretreatment of adding CO2-NW and O2-NW (PCO2-MDW 
and PO2-MDW) compared with DW soaking (PDW-MDW). As discussed in 
Section 3.1.1, the higher peak daily methane yield after soaking in NW 
could be attributed to the higher VFAs content than that after soaking in 
DW. Although the daily methane yield was affected by soaking pre­
treatment with different types of NW, the cumulative methane yields 
were comparable between the NW and the DW soaking treatments. 
Therefore, sole soaking in NW only increased the peak of the daily 
methane yield, but resulted in comparable the cumulative methane yield 
to DW. 
To achieve higher biogas production, this study explored the effect of 
NW addition on both the soaking pretreatment and the successive AD 
process on the biogas production of rice straw. The cumulative methane 
yields matrix (Pi × Mj) is presented in Table 3. For rice straw pretreated 
with different types of water (DW, N2-NW, CO2-NW, and O2-NW) as both 
soaking agent and AD accelerants, the cumulative methane yield ranged 
from 287.0 to 313.9 mL/gVS. The Pi-MCO2 and Pi-MO2 treatments (with 
CO2-NW and O2-NW) as AD accelerants significantly increased the cu­
mulative methane yield compared with the Pi-MDW treatment (p < 0.05).

±1.7 mL/gVS), followed by the PCO2-MO2 treatment (311.4±1.9 mL/ 
gVS). The daily and cumulative methane yields of rice straw treated with 
different types of water (DW, N2-NW, CO2-NW, and O2-NW) as both 
soaking pretreatment and AD accelerant are illustrated in Fig. 3. The 
highest daily methane yield was observed in the application of CO2-NW 
as an AD accelerant (Pi × MCO2) within 3 days, regardless of the type of 
NW used as a soaking pretreatment. This meant that the addition of CO2- 
NW as an AD accelerant was beneficial for the hydrolysis and acidifi­
cation of organic matter. 
In this study, the addition of CO2-NW during the soaking process 
increased the cumulative methane yield by 14.2% compared with the 
untreated group without soaking. When considering only the difference 
between soaking pretreatment in NW and DW during soaking (PCO2- 
MDW treatment compared with PDW-MDW treatment), the cumulative 
yield increment was extremely limited (+0.9%). Interestingly, the 
addition of CO2-NW during the soaking and AD processes could increase 
the cumulative yield by 21.4% and 7.3%, respectively, compared with 
the untreated group and PDW-MDW treatment. The increase in methane 
production with the addition of CO2-NW in this study was similar to that 
reported in previous studies. Wang et al. (2019) found that the cumu­
lative methane yield of waste activated sludge increased by 16% after 
the addition of CO2-NW as an AD accelerant compared with DW treat­
ment. Fan et al. (2020a) revealed that the addition of CO2-NW as AD 
accelerant resulted in an increase of 20.8% in the cumulative methane 
yield of swine manure compared with the DW treatment. The studies 
also reported that a higher cumulative methane yield was achieved by 
adding H2-NW, air-NW, and CO2-NW to AD process; however, the 
addition of N2-NW resulted in only a slight increase in yield. The in­
crease in methane production might be attributed to the addition of NW 
as AD accelerant, which could enhance the enzyme and microbial ac­
tivity of hydrolysis and methanogenesis. This study also proved that 
addition of NW at the soaking pretreatment and AD processes could 
enhance methane production and improve the efficiency of the AD 
system. 
The highest methane production was obtained with the addition of 
CO2-NW as an AD accelerant, which might be due to the provision of 
exogenous CO2 as a substrate to increase methane production. In a 
previous study, CO2 was injected into a sewage sludge pilot-scale AD 
reactor, resulting in an increase of 6% in methane yield compared with 
the untreated group (Muntau et al., 2021). The higher methane yield 
might be attributed to the stimulation hydrogenotrophic (Wang et al., 
2020a) and acetoclastic (Baj´on Fern´andez et al., 2015) methanogenesis 
pathways under CO2-enriched conditions. Due to the high mass transfer 
efficiency of gas-liquid NW, the CO2-NW applied in this study might lead 
to a greater improvement of biogas production compared with direct 
injection of CO2; therefore, further research was necessary. 
The modified Gompertz model was used to fit the kinetic charac­
teristics of methane yield with different NW. The kinetic characteristics 
and the digestion time T80 (reaching 80% of P0) are shown in Fig. 3 
(embedded table). According to the results, all groups were fitted well 
(R2 >0.984). For PCO2-MCO2 treatment, P0 was 303.5±4.5 mL/gVS, 
thereby being 22.6% and 9.4% higher than untreated (247.6±3.8 mL/ 
gVS) and PDW-MDW (277.3±6.2 mL/gVS), respectively. In addition, 
using NW as AD accelerant decreased λ compared with DW, implying 
faster methane production in rice straw AD. 
It is worth noting that the air-dried rice straw used in this study had a 
high lignocellulose content and lignification degree compared with 
those of freshly harvested straw, which seriously hindered the AD pro­
cess (Cai et al., 2021). The improvement in methane production was not 
obviously evident that using sole NW soaking as a gentle pretreatment 
compared with DW soaking. In addition, according to previous research, 
the enhancement mechanism of AD process by adding NW was to 
enhance the activity of microorganism (Fan et al., 2020b; Wang et al., 
2020b). As discussed in section 3.1.1, this study might only stimulate 
epiphytic microorganism in air-dry crop straw during soaking process 
without exogenous inoculated hydrolytic bacteria. Therefore, this study 
speculate that the combined application of inoculum (exogenous hy­
drolytic bacteria) and NW will be beneficial for the methane formation 
and hydrolysis. 
3.3. Microbial community analysis 
As discussed in Section 3.2, using NW as an AD accelerant had a 
greater effect on the cumulative methane yield than using as a soaking 
agent. Therefore, this study selected the treatment of PDW-MDW, PDW- 
MN2, PDW-MCO2, PDW-MO2, and PCO2-MCO2 to analyze microbial com­
munity influenced by the NW. The Shannon index of bacteria, indicating 
microbial community diversity, was relatively high in the treatment 
using CO2-NW or O2-NW as an AD accelerant. This result indicated that 
CO2-NW and O2-NW could increase bacterial diversity and accelerate 
the rate-limiting hydrolysis step to achieve efficient biogas production 
(see supplementary material). This observation was confirmed by the 
change in the Simpson index of bacteria, which was negatively corre­
lated with diversity. Interestingly, the Shannon index of archaea 
exhibited a completely opposite trend to that of bacteria. Decreased 
archaeal diversity was observed in the treatments using CO2-NW or O2- 
NW as an AD accelerant (see supplementary material). This could be due 
to the added CO2-NW and O2-NW in the AD system promoting the 
succession of microbial population (Zhang et al., 2022). It is worth 
noting that the decrease in archaeal diversity did not decrease the 
methane yield. The reasons for the decrease in archaeal diversity 
observed in this study need to be further studied. 
The relative abundance of bacterial community abundant at the 
phylum level is shown in Fig. 4a. The dominant phyla in all treatments 
were Firmicutes, Synergistota, Bacteroidota, Caldatribacteriota, and Chlor­
oflexi. Firmicutes was the most abundant phyla among all treatments, 
while it had been previously reported that Firmicutes played an impor­
tant role in the degradation of lignocellulose to produce VFAs (Ma et al., 
2022). Interestingly, in the PCO2-MCO2 treatment, the relative abundance

of Bacteroidota and Chloroflexi increased compared with that in the other 
treatments. Bacteroidota had the ability to convert polysaccharides into 
organic acids (Wang et al., 2021a). And Chloroflexi was associated with 
the degradation of butyrate and refractory organic matter (Shao et al., 
2022). It was possible that the addition of CO2-NW during soaking 
(PCO2-MCO2) promoted the enrichment of Bacteroidota and Chloroflexi, 
thereby enhancing the degradation of rice straw and production of 
organic acid. However, compared with DW (PDW-MDW), adding NW as 
an AD accelerant (PDW-MN2, PDW-MCO2, and PDW-MO2) did not signifi­
cantly affect the bacterial community composition. 
The relative abundance of archaeal community at the genus level is 
shown in Fig. 4b by adding NW as an AD accelerant. The major genera 
were 
Methanosaeta, 
Methanolinea, 
norank_c_Bathyarchaeia, 
Meth­
anomethylovorans, and Methanobacterium. The relative abundances of 
Methanosaeta in the treatment of PDW-MDW, PDW-MN2, PDW-MCO2, PDW- 
MO2, and PCO2-MCO2 were 44.2%, 56.5%, 56.6%, 65.2%, and 67.3%, 
respectively. Methanosaeta was an obligate acetoclastic methanogen and 
was sensitive to high acetic acid concentrations in AD reactors (Ma et al., 
2022; Wang et al., 2020a). This means that using NW as an AD accel­
erant could promote the activity of acetoclastic methanogens. The high 
relative abundance of Methanolinea, a typical hydrogenotrophic 
methanogen, increased after the addition of CO2-NW, indicating the 
enhancement of the hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis pathway by 
CO2-NW (Wang et al., 2020a). Norank_c_Bathyarchaeia could utilize 
carbohydrates, VFAs, methane, and other organic matter to produce 
acetyl-CoA which was subsequently consumed by Bathyarchaeota (Xie 
et al., 2022). The higher relative abundance of Norank_c_Bathyarchaeia 
might be the reason for the lower methane yield in the PDW-MDW 
treatment. 
Therefore, the application of CO2-NW and O2-NW as AD accelerants 
promoted the growth of acetoclastic methanogens in this study which 
might be the reason for the increased biogas production observed. These 
results and discussion were based on the microorganisms of the sample 
inoculum this time; however, differences may occur under different 
inoculation conditions. This will be further discussed in future research 
on the optimization of related operating condition. 
4. Conclusion 
The double effect of NW as soaking agent and AD accelerant was 
investigated for rice straw. The biomethane yields increased by 11.0%– 
21.4% after the application of NW as soaking agent and AD accelerant 
compared with that in untreated straw. The VFAs concentration 
increased to 78.9%–214.4% by adding NW soaking. CO2-NW showed 
the better performance compared other groups. This study suggested 
that using NW could enhance two-step AD process. Coupling of inoc­
ulum and NW in the hydrolysis process will be further studied to reveal 
the difference with traditional hydrolysis method.
